newsitem.title: JAPAN: POLL-Japan June industry output seen down 2.8 pct. [CORRECTED 05:53 GMT]
newsitem.headline: POLL-Japan June industry output seen down 2.8 pct. [CORRECTED 05:53 GMT]

text.p: Japan's industrial output is expected to have fallen 2.8 percent in June from the previous month after a large increase in May, an average of economists' forecasts showed on Monday.

Economists' predictions for industrial output ranged from a fall of 1.2 percent to a fall of 4.0 percent, compared with the Ministry of International Trade and Industry's (MITI) forecast of a 2.6 percent drop in manufacturers' output.
(Corrects to show economists were forecasting industrial output and the ministry manufacturers' output.)
MITI does not forecast overall industrial output, only output for manufacturers, which is a key component of the overall indicator.
The data will be announced 1.30 p.m. (0430 GMT) on Wednesday. Much of the market focus is expected to be on MITI's forecasts for July and August.
MITI has given a preliminary forecast of a 0.9 rise in manufacturers' output for July.
Economists who expected a large fall in June made their forecasts after a larger-than-expected revised increase of 4.5 percent in May against a preliminary 3.8 percent rise.
Declines in output expected among machinery sectors and raw materials as well as the steel sector were cited as key factors in pushing down overall production in June.
But those that saw only a small month-on-month contraction said that manufacturers' had not been doing too badly with the car sector especially strong.
In particular, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell which saw a fall of 1.2 percent from a month earlier, pointed to a 16.1 percent year-on-year rise in Japan's vehicle output for June.
Economists agreed, however, that despite the expected fall for June, industrial production continued to be on a recovery track.

"It's not really that low a figure, it's still high in year-on-year terms," said Hiroshi Miyazaki at Yamaichi Research, which predicts a fall of 4.0 percent from May but a rise of 7.0 percent compared with the same period a year ago. The following is a breakdown of economists' forecasts:
